Faster-WAM in LeRobot: keep the visual depth, shrink the action decoder

Faster-WAM cuts a world action model's action expert to one layer. I added it to LeRobot behind opt-in flags and timed it on an A100 with random weights.

October 21, 20266 min readUpdated October 27, 2026

world-action-modelslerobotkv-cacheflow-matching

Suppose we want a robot policy to produce its next 32 actions. In Fast-WAM, a video model helps learn the task by predicting video during training. At inference, it processes the current image once and saves intermediate representations from all 30 layers. The action decoder then refines a noisy action chunk ten times. Each refinement passes through another 30 layers. That is a lot of repeated work before the robot gets its actions. How much of that decoder can we remove?

Faster-WAM takes it down to one layer. But now we have a question: which of the 30 visual layers should our one action layer read? We could use only the last one. Faster-WAM instead learns how much to take from each. Follow the same chunk through both paths:

Paper-reported task success (%). LIBERO contains simulated tabletop tasks; LIBERO-Plus perturbs those scenes. Changes accumulate down the rows. Fast-WAM scores come from earlier papers; only the final configuration is a three-run mean.
ConfigurationLIBEROLIBERO-Plus
Fast-WAM, 30 action layers97.651.5
One action layer, final video cache97.760.3
+ learned cache fusion98.068.7
+ conditioning through video only97.877.6
+ positional retraction98.378.3

I find the first ablation particularly interesting: even one action layer reading only the final video cache retains LIBERO success. The complete system improves LIBERO-Plus, although RoboTwin 2.0 success falls from 91.8% to 90.5%. In LeRobot, the integration exposes four opt-in settings, shown below. Start from a Fast-WAM checkpoint, then fine-tune the one-layer action decoder, the weights that mix the visual caches, and the video model together. Flipping the settings on an existing checkpoint leaves that learning undone.

config = FastWAMConfig(
    action_expert_layers=1,
    lite_kv_fusion=True,
    retracted_1d_rope=True,
    world_model_only_conditioning=True,
)
Milliseconds per 32-action chunk. Paper and local timings use different GPUs and timing boundaries: the paper excludes tokenization and transfers and sums separately timed baseline components. Local runs used random video-model and action-expert weights with the actual VAE image encoder and text encoder. They measure execution speed; trained-policy quality, local LIBERO performance and robot behavior were untested, and the merged implementation was not timed.

Timing method and additional profiling

The local report used one A100-SXM4-80GB host on Hugging Face Jobs, 12 vCPUs, PyTorch 2.11.0, CUDA 13.0 and LeRobot commit 50dffcf. Batch size was one, images were 224 × 448, and denoising used ten iterations. Execution was eager, with TF32 and compilation disabled. Each precision used 100 shuffled model pairs, timed from tokenization through actions returned to CPU.

Within-session 95% bootstrap speedup intervals were 2.50–2.52× for float32 and 5.33–5.36× for bfloat16. Across sessions, speedups changed from 2.66× to 2.51× and 5.10× to 5.34× respectively. Session variability exceeded those narrow intervals.

Fast-WAM's eager denoiser slowed from about 493 ms in float32 to 797 ms in bfloat16 despite faster encoding and prefill. Another session replayed the unchanged bfloat16 baseline through a CUDA graph: reported whole-chunk latency fell from 868.2 to 283.5 ms with bit-identical outputs. That intervention removes dispatch and temporary-allocation costs together; their individual contributions remain unresolved. No paired compiled-model comparison was reported.

Phase timings and the widget came from a separate 20-chunk CUDA-event run; kernel counts came from a profiler run. Underlying profiling records are unpublished.

Integration context: LeRobot issue. The source reports an independent implementation with no code taken from the authors' repository, whose license it characterizes as noncommercial. The Faster-WAM paper discussed here is 2608.02365v2; 2608.04404 is a separate paper sharing the name.

The local bfloat16 run was about 5.3× faster end to end. Profiling counted 29,020 GPU kernel launches per baseline chunk versus 770 for Faster-WAM, so the measured gain includes far less overhead from launching GPU work. The 30-fold reduction in cache reads therefore describes work, not an equivalent latency speedup. Once the decoder shrinks, the next optimization target moves: in the separate phase run, Faster-WAM denoising took 23.7 ms, while text encoding took about 42 ms and visual prefill about 88 ms. We can now spend more time preparing the scene than deciding the actions. Encoding, prefill and compilation become useful places to look next.
